analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas leasing along the Atlantic, Pacific, and Alaska coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in House committees from November 1989 until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred the Interior Department from issuing any new oil or gas leases on submerged federal lands within roughly 50 to 175 miles of the coasts of every Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf-facing state from Florida to Maine, plus Oregon, Washington, and Alaska. It would have kept leases already in effect, but canceled certain leases in areas off Florida and Alaska's North Aleutian Basin, with compensation to the leaseholders under existing law. It never advanced past its committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents and economies built on fishing and tourism, which bear the risk of oil spills, along with anyone who benefits from keeping new drilling off most of the nation's coastline. States that had fought federal leasing plans would have gained a permanent legal shield.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and fishing and tourism economies

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited the Interior Secretary from issuing any new lease, permit, or license for oil or gas exploration or extraction on submerged lands within 100 miles of most Atlantic and Pacific coasts and within 100 miles of Alaska's coast [S2][S3].

It protected existing areas previously covered by leasing moratoria off Florida, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and Alaska, putting those temporary bans into law [S3].

It directed the Secretary to cancel leases in areas south of 26 degrees north latitude off Florida and in the North Aleutian Basin, entitling leaseholders to compensation under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry, which would lose access to vast stretches of federal offshore acreage for exploration, and taxpayers to the extent leaseholders whose leases were canceled are owed compensation. Existing leaseholders would keep their rights, so current production would not stop.

drawbacks.text: The bill keeps every lease, permit, and license in effect on enactment, so drilling under existing leases would continue and the ban applies only to new leasing [S2][S3].

Cancelling certain existing leases requires compensating the holders, and the bill directs the Interior Secretary to report on compensation options including royalty credits, which could shift costs to the Treasury [S2][S3].
Excluding all drilling from these waters reduces potential domestic oil and gas supply, a cost supporters would have to weigh against spill protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is broad but incomplete: it locks in a permanent ban on new leasing across nearly all non-Gulf offshore waters, which protects coastlines from spill risk, while grandfathering existing leases and requiring compensation for a small set of canceled ones. The main gap is that it leaves current drilling untouched and keeps the Gulf of Mexico's Central and Western planning areas open entirely [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, but no committee ever reported it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on November 20, 1989, with 24 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs and concurrently to the House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries [S5].
On March 16, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Panama Canal/Outer Continental Shelf, and executive comments were requested from the Interior Department, Treasury, and EPA [S5].
By the end it had 72 cosponsors, 62 Democrats and 10 Republicans, but no committee reported the bill and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas producers, who kept open the possibility of new federal leasing off Atlantic, Pacific, and Alaska coasts, and leaseholders whose rights were left untouched. Coastal communities gained nothing from the bill's failure, though moratoria were kept through other means.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban new offshore oil and gas leasing off the Atlantic, Pacific, and Alaska coasts.

against.name: House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup in the roughly 13 months it held it.

against.name: Interior Department (George H.W. Bush administration)
against.role: Executive agency whose leasing programs the bill would stop
against.what_they_did: Executive comment was requested from Interior; the administration of the day supported continuing offshore lease sales.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic, but the bill had real bipartisan support with 62 Democratic and 10 Republican cosponsors; no floor vote was ever taken to show a party split.

industries.note: The bill would have closed nearly all new federal offshore acreage outside the central and western Gulf of Mexico to leasing and canceled certain existing leases. Its failure kept access open for future lease sales.

Both industries bear the spill and infrastructure risk of offshore drilling along the coasts the bill would have shielded; the bill's death left them without the permanent legal protection it offered.

Most leases in effect at enactment would have been grandfathered, while leaseholders in the Florida and North Aleutian Basin areas specified would have had leases canceled with compensation under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.
